book:11300802.description: 'Ah, Hippothales, I said; what a noble and really perfect love you have found! I wish that you would favour me with the exhibition which you have been making to the rest of the company, and then I shall be able to judge whether you know what a lover ought to say about his love, either to the youth himself, or to others.'

Walter Pater cites the Lysis as a dialogue that embodies the purely Greek element that attracted Winckelmann.

book:21734345.description: Crito is a short but important dialogue by the ancient Greek philosopher Plato. It is a conversation between Socrates and his wealthy friend Crito regarding justice, injustice, and the appropriate response to injustice. Socrates thinks that injustice may not be answered with injustice, and refuses Crito's offer to finance his escape from prison...

book:6091408.description: These new translations of the Defence of Socrates, the Euthyphro, and the Crito present Plato's remarkable dramatizations of the momentous events surrounding the trial of Socrates in 399 BC, on charges of irreligion and corrupting the young. They form a dramatic and thematic sequence, raising fundamental questions about the basis of moral, religious, legal, and political obligation. The Introduction provides a stimulating philosophical and historical analysis of these texts, complemented by useful explanato...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists several works attributed to Plato.

John Ruskin cites Plato's 'Alcibiades I' as a perfect example of the four cardinal virtues in education.

book:7614733.description: One of the very first books that discuses philosophy of logic. Coming from a time when man was in the initial stages of differing between thinking and acting, philosophy and logic, this is one of the, masterpieces by Plato. Thought-provoking!
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Plato's dialogue 'Euthydemus' for the claim that Protagoras first used the reasonings of Antisthenes.

commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that Plato mentions his teacher Dionysius in the dialogue Rival Lovers.

book:16655575.description: Protagoras presents a vivid picture of the crisis of fifth-century Greek thought, in which traditional values and conceptions of man were subjected both to the criticism of the Sophists and to the far more radical criticism of Socrates. The dialogue deals with many themes which are central to the ethical theories which Plato developed under the influence of Socrates, notably the nature of human excellence, the relation of knowledge to right conduct, and the place of pleasure in the good life.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Plato's 'Protagoras' for including Myson among the seven sages.
Diogenes Laertius notes that Plato mentions Pittacus's saying in his dialogue Protagoras.

book:14458321.description: ...It seems impossible to separate by any exact line the genuine writings of Plato from the spurious. The only external evidence to them which is of much value is that of Aristotle; for the Alexandrian catalogues of a century later include manifest forgeries. Even the value of the Aristotelian authority is a good deal impaired by the uncertainty concerning the date and authorship of the writings which are ascribed to him. And several of the citations of Aristotle omit the name of Plato, and some of them omi...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists several works attributed to Plato.
Plutarch references Plato's dialog 'Menexenus' as a source for the historical claim that Aspasia was known for teaching rhetoric.

book:6560768.description: In the Meno, Anytus had parted from Socrates with the significant words: 'That in any city, and particularly in the city of Athens, it is easier to do men harm than to do them good;' and Socrates was anticipating another opportunity of talking with him. In the Euthyphro, Socrates is awaiting his trial for impiety. But before the trial begins, Plato would like to put the world on their trial, and convince them of ignorance in that very matter touching which Socrates is accused. An incident which may perhaps....
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists several works attributed to Plato.

book:340960.description: Set immediately prior to the trial and execution of Socrates in 399 BC, Theaetetus shows the great philosopher considering the nature of knowledge itself, in a debate with the geometrician Theodorus and his young follower Theaetetus. Their dialogue covers many questions, such as: is knowledge purely subjective, composed of the ever-changing flow of impressions we receive from the outside world? Is it better thought of as 'true belief'? Or is it, as many modern philosophers argue, 'justified true belief', in...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists several works attributed to Plato.
Diogenes Laertius cites Plato's dialogue 'Theætetus' as the source for Protagoras's doctrine that the soul is the senses.

book:web_1df9d2e4.description: A short Socratic dialogue attributed to Plato, focusing on the theme of justice and the limitations of rhetorical persuasion.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that some begin with the Clitophon.

book:26188710.description: PLATO (428/427 bc - 348/347 bc), was a Classical Greek philosopher, mathematician, writer of philosophical dialogues, and founder of the Academy in Athens, the first institution of higher learning in the western world.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius classifies the Cratylus as a logical dialogue by Plato.

book:web_5e9cfa40.description: Plato's dialogue on the ideal statesman, also known as the Statesman (Politicus), listed among logical works by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius classifies the Politics as a logical dialogue by Plato.

book:4590736.description: Ils sont allonges sur des lits et parlent de l'Amour et de la Beaute. Leurs discours se succedent, parfois se repondent : car il y a plusieurs Amours et plusieurs manieres de desirer le Beau. A ces hommes vivant en un temps et un lieu ou l'education des garcons est indissociable de la sexualite qui regle les rapports du maitre et du disciple, une etrangere, Diotime, oppose un modele feminin de la procreation du savoir. A travers elle, Socrate dessine les etapes de l'apprentissage du philosophe capable de se...
commentaries: William James quotes Plato's 'Banquet' (Symposium) to illustrate the ascent to absolute Beauty.
William James cites Plato's 'Symposium' as a source, referencing the Jowett translation.

book:13611921.description:
Plato (circa 427-347 B.C.) was a famous Greek philosopher who is largely responsible for Western philosophy as we know it today. Plato was mentored by Socrates and much of his writings were based off of dialogues between Socrates and others. Plato also was the teacher of many philosophers with the most famous amongst them being Arisotle.
This version of Plato's The Letters includes a table of contents.
commentaries: Plutarch references Plato's epistles as evidence that Dion was turned out and did not leave the court voluntarily to wage war.

book:web_8f1014a2.description: Plato's dialogue on the ideal statesman and classification of constitutions, often referred to as 'Politicus'. The passage cited (Stephanus 302c) discusses six forms of government (kingship, tyranny, aristocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and its bad form) alongside the ideal polity.
commentaries: Polybius notes that Aristotle's classification was derived from Plato's Politics.

book:web_c639bf10.description: Platonic dialogue on the nature of love, also known as 'The Banquet of Plato', featuring Socrates, Alcibiades, and Agathon.
commentaries: Voltaire refers to Plato's Symposium as a philosophical source on love.

book:web_54695c27.description: Julius Caesar's firsthand account of the Gallic Wars, written around 58–50 BCE.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Caesar's work as a source.

book:web_e319c371.description: A lost polemical work written by Julius Caesar in response to Cicero's eulogy of Cato the Younger, criticizing Cato's actions and character.
commentaries: Plutarch mentions that Caesar wrote a book against Cato, which criticized Cato's mistrustfulness.
Plutarch mentions Caesar's composition of 'Anti-Cato' as a response to a panegyric on Cato.

book:pg1091.description: From its first pages the book recognizes the intimate connections between heroism and myth. Beginning with the legends of Odin, lord of the Nordic gods, Carlyle describes major forms that heroism can take: in god, poet, warrior, priest, prophet, and king.
commentaries: The footnote directs the reader to Carlyle's work for a discussion on the subject.

book:web_878137d4.description: A series of lectures discussing the role of heroes in history, originally published in 1841.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson references Carlyle's published lectures as a related work on great men.

book:web_f339d96e.description: English Anglican priest and theologian, author of the influential work 'Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity'.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites Hooker's 'Ecclesiastical Polity' as an example of a judicious author who anticipated complaints of obscurity when tracing a subject to its highest source.

book:web_52f833b9.description: Book by Joseph Butler, first published in 1736, arguing by analogy for the consistency of natural and revealed religion.
commentaries: Charles Darwin quotes Butler's Analogy of Revealed Religion as an epigraph.

book:pg785.description: Martin Ferguson Smith's work on Lucretius is both well known and highly regarded. However, his 1969 translation of De Rerum Natura--long out of print--is virtually unknown. Readers will share our excitement in the discovery of this accurate and fluent prose rendering. For this edition, Professor Smith provides a revised translation, new Introduction, headnotes and bibliography.

book:43958.description: A highly influential figure in the Church of England, John Henry Newman stunned the Anglican community in 1843, when he left his position as vicar of St. Mary's, Oxford, to join the Roman Catholic church. Perhaps no one took greater offense than Protestant clergyman Charles Kingsley, whose scathing attacks against Newman's faith and honor inspired this brilliant response. Apologia Pro Vita Sua,Newman's spiritual autobiography, explores the depths and nature of Christianity with flowing prose and a conversat...
commentaries: Matthew Arnold references Dr. Newman's Apology as a source to understand the Oxford movement's opposition to liberalism.
William James quotes Newman's autobiographical reflections on dogma and his relationship with ecclesiastical authority.

book:web_d4949d0a.description: A series of theological lectures by John Henry Newman, first published in 1838, exploring the doctrine of justification in Christian theology.
commentaries: William James references Newman's work as containing a passage that illustrates an aesthetic approach to Christianity.

book:449250.description: The issues that John Henry Newman raised--the place of religion and moral values in the university setting, the competing claims of liberal and professional education, the character of the academic community, the cultural role of literature, the relation of religion and science--have provoked discussion from Newman's time to our own.
commentaries: William James cites Cardinal Newman's The Idea of a University as a work that expresses disdain for sentiment and insists on theology as a science.

book:8254877.description: The emperor Marcus Aurelius, the proverbial philosopher-king, produced in Greek a Roman manual of piety, the Meditations, whose impact has been felt for ages since. Here, for our age, is his great work presented in its entirety, strongly introduced and freshly, elegantly translated.
commentaries: Matthew Arnold compares Bishop Wilson's Maxims to the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, noting its sincerity and first-hand quality.

book:547746.description: Written in 397 A.D., Confessions is the autobiography of Augustine of Hippo, a moving and profound record of a human soul and its struggles toward salvation. The most widely read of all his works, it not only tells the story of Augustine's struggle in the faith, but also his love for Jesus Christ.
commentaries: Matthew Arnold cites St. Augustine's Confessions as an incomparable literary monument of early Christian asceticism.
Augustine of Hippo cites Augustine's Confessions as a reference for Augustine's own childhood experiences.
Augustine of Hippo notes that Augustine published an idea in his Confessions, which he later retracted.
Ralph Waldo Emerson mentions St. Augustine and identifies his work _Confessions_.
The footnote references Augustine's 'Confessions', Book I.
William James cites Augustine's Confessions as a source.

book:pg45304.description:
One of the great cornerstones in the history of Christian philosophy, The City of God provides an insightful interpretation of the development of modern Western society and the origin of most Western thought. Contrasting earthly and heavenly cities--representing the omnipresent struggle between good and evil--Augustine explores human history in its relation to all eternity. In Thomas Merton's words, "The City of God is the autobiography of the Church written by the most Catholic of her great saints."
This M...
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references St. Augustine's City of God as providing an analysis of Cicero's work.
James George Frazer cites Augustine's City of God as a source.
William James quotes Augustine's City of God to illustrate early Christian teleological speculation about natural phenomena.

book:pg3296.description:
ROSE ZARELLI is done confessing because confessions are for people who have done something wrong. And I haven't done anything wrong. Here, I'll prove it to you.
1) After my mother got that call, I "borrowed" her car. (Because you can't steal your mother's car, can you?) I don't really remember driving downtown, but I do remember...
2) ...getting past the bouncer at Dizzy's (I mean, it's his job to spot a fake ID, so that's on him)...
3) ...and then later, telling my mother the truth about the bar but lying....

book:web_474693da.description: An early lost work by Augustine, written around 386 AD, on aesthetics and ethics, mentioned in his Confessions.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo mentions writing books on the subject of 'the fair and fit,' which he later refers to as having been dedicated to the orator Hierius.

book:web_a05dd9ad.description: A philosophical dialogue between Augustine and his son Adeodatus, exploring the nature of language and teaching.
commentaries: Augustine mentions a book he authored, 'The Master', which records a dialogue between himself and his friend Adeodatus in his sixteenth year.

book:6397530.description: At the end of his life (ca. 426-428) Augustine revisited his previous works in chronological order. The English translation of the title has led some to assume that at the end of his career, Augustine retreated from his earlier theological positions. In fact, the Latin title literally means 're-treatments" (not "Retractions") and though in this work Augustine suggested what he would have said differently, it provides little in the way of actual "retraction." It does, however, give the reader a rare picture....
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references his own work Retractations to correct a previous statement about a miraculous appearance.

book:web_a1dcf057.description: A letter (epistle) written by Augustine of Hippo to Deogratias, a deacon of Carthage, discussing the nature of the soul and other theological matters. Part of Augustine's collected letters.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references his own prior works for comparison or further reading.

book:19129596.description: The Memorabilia Recollections of Socrates By Xenophon Translated by H. G. Dakyns Complete Edition Memorabilia is a collection of Socratic dialogues by Xenophon, a student of Socrates. The lengthiest and most famous of Xenophon's Socratic writings, the Memorabilia is essentially an apologia, defense, of Socrates, differing from both Xenophon's Apology of Socrates to the Jury and Plato's Apology mainly in that the Apologies present Socrates as defending himself before the jury, whereas the former presents Xen...
commentaries: Arnold refers to Xenophon's Memorabilia as the source for a Socratic saying about self-perfection and happiness.
Diogenes Laertius describes Zeno reading and being delighted by the second book of Xenophon's Memorabilia.

book:7946890.description:
Hiero (Greek: Ieron, Hieron) is a minor work by Xenophon, set as a dialog between Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, & the lyric poet Simonides about 474 BCE. In it Xenophon argues that a tyrant doesn't have any more access to happiness than a private person.
The dialog--like many of Xenophon's works--doesn't receive much scholarly attention today. However, it was the nominal subject of Leo Strauss' analysis On Tyranny, which initiated his famous dialog with Alexandre Kojeve on the role of philosophy in politics.
commentaries: Niccolò Machiavelli cites Xenophon's treatise as a source to confirm his views on the hatred of tyrants and love of freedom.

book:20087887.description: Written in the early fourth century BCE by a gentleman and soldier from Athens, "Cyropaedia" is an account of Cyrus the Great that escapes a simple genre placement. It is a sort of historical, political, biographical, fictional romance, encapsulating the sweeping type of narrative characteristic of Xenophon's works. The overall portrait of Cyrus is artistic, offering glimpses of this huge figure's character. Organized into eight books, the entire life of Cyrus the Great is told, from his descent and educati...
commentaries: Niccolò Machiavelli cites Xenophon's account of Cyrus to illustrate how the chase is a mimic representation of war, and to support the argument that hunting is useful and honourable for great men.
Pliny the Elder cites Xenophon's work to qualify an account of Cyrus's memory.
Plutarch cites Xenophon's words on the value of preserving good men's casual sayings.
Suetonius mentions that Caesar, upon reading this account, deprecated a lingering death and wished for a sudden one.

book:20657855.description: In The Persian Expedition, Xenophon, a young Athenian noble who sought his destiny abroad, provides an enthralling eyewitness account of the attempt by a Greek mercenary army - the Ten Thousand - to help Prince Cyrus overthrow his brother and take the Persian throne. When the Greeks were then betrayed by their Persian employers, they were forced to march home through hundreds of miles of difficult terrain - adrift in a hostile country and under constant attack from the unforgiving Persians and warlike tribe...
commentaries: Plutarch reports that Xenophon, present at the battle, described it as the hardest fought he had seen.

book:7774527.description: "Hellenica is Xenophon's chronicle of the history of the Greeks, or the "Hellenes" from 411 to 359 BCE. It is a continuation of Thucydides' narrative, "History of the Peloponnesian War." This history covers the last seven years of the war, and its aftermath. It is one of the few surviving narratives from this period and is generally considered to be the most authoritative. The author Xenophon was born in Athens about 430BCE. It may be inferred from passages in the Hellenica that he fought at Arginusae (406)...
commentaries: Polybius references Xenophon's 'Hellenica' as a source.
Polybius cites Xenophon's Hellenica as a source for a Greek phrase.
Polybius references Xenophon's Hellenica as a source for the account of Epaminondas's march.

book:214441.description: Green Lion Press has prepared a new one-volume edition of T.L. Heath's translation of the thirteen books of Euclid's Elements. In keeping with Green Lion's design commitment, diagrams have been placed on every spread for convenient reference while working through the proofs; running heads on every page indicate both Euclid's book number and proposition numbers for that page; and adequate space for notes is allowed between propositions and around diagrams. The all-new index has built into it a glossary of Eu...

commentaries: James George Frazer cites Preller's Greek Mythology as a source.

book:1629151.description:
The Second Epistle to the Corinthians [NICNT] illuminates the historical background of the church at Corinth and clarifies the meaning of Paul's passionate letter both for those first-century Christians and for today.
Barnett assumes and offers argument for the unity of the letter and takes the view that Paul is addressing the issue of triumphalism in Corinth expressed by the newly arrived missioners who portray Paul as inferior to themselves. It is also endemic among the Corinthians and according to Barnet...
commentaries: Matthew Arnold compares St. Paul's argumentation in the Epistle to the Corinthians with Plato's in the Phaedo, finding both inadequate.

book:12292772.description: A masterpiece of German literature, this is the only edition in print in the English-speaking world of the complete Wilhelm Meister--both Wilhelm Meister's Years of Apprenticeshipand Wilhelm Meister's Years of TravelSpring had appeared in its full magnificence--an untimely storm that had been threatening all day broke turbulently on the heights, the rain moved over the countryside, the sun came out again in its radiance, and against the grey background the splendid rainbow became visible. Wilhelm was riding...

Walter Pater references Goethe's novel Wilhelm Meister, specifically the character of the Schoene Seele, as an example of a phase of life that Goethe's larger vision could encompass and move beyond.
Leo Tolstoy cites Folgeldt's argument that a moral demand on art would exclude Goethe's Wilhelm Meister, which is part of the accepted art canon.

book:web_d947a89c.description: A novel by Goethe, sequel to 'Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship', published in expanded form in 1829. The passage cited refers to the Society of the Tower's rule of self-restriction.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle cites Goethe's work 'Meister's Travels' to illustrate a principle about self-restraint.

book:web_d065b697.description: An epistolary novel by Goethe about a young artist's unrequited love and eventual suicide, highly influential in the Sturm und Drang movement.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge reports that the person praised Goethe's novel above his plays.

book:1768990.description: In dem Versdrama >>Torquato Tasso<<, einem der literarischen Ertrage der Italienreise, schuf Goethe das erste regelrechte Kunstlerdrama der Weltliteratur. Dabei tragt der Kunstlertypus, der in der Figur des Tasso gezeichnet wird, neben der Genialitat auch Zuge von Melancholie und Labilitat und avanciert so zum Psychogramm eines schon modernen Dichters. (Amazon)
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson references Goethe's play as an example of true tragedy.

book:web_d426797d.description: Autobiography of Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, originally published in German as 'Aus meinem Leben: Dichtung und Wahrheit' (1811–1833).
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson discusses Goethe's autobiography, noting its expression of the idea that a man exists for culture.

book:web_7f3797a8.description: An autobiographical chronicle by Goethe, originally titled 'Tag- und Jahreshefte', covering his life from 1749 to 1822, first published in 1830 as part of his collected works.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson notes that these works by Goethe share the same interest in his relationship with other remarkable minds.

book:web_d57ed0d5.description: Autobiographical work by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, covering his early life and literary development.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson discusses how the idea of knowing the history and destiny of man governs the selection of incidents in Goethe's autobiography, rather than external importance.

book:18225.description:
By the time Goethe's "Theory of Colours" appeared in 1810, the wavelength theory of light and color had been firmly established. To Goethe, the theory was the result of mistaking an incidental result for an elemental principle. Far from pretending to a knowledge of physics, he insisted that such knowledge was an actual hindrance to understanding. He based his conclusions exclusively upon exhaustive personal observation of the phenomena of color.
Of his own theory, Goethe was supremely confident: "From the p...
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson notes that the historical part of this work by Goethe shares the same interest, rapidly noting Kepler, Roger Bacon, Galileo, Newton, Voltaire, etc.

book:web_920ad399.description: An account of Goethe's experiences during the French Revolutionary Wars.
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson notes that these works by Goethe share the same interest in his relationship with other remarkable minds.

book:832491.description: In 1786, when he was already the acknowledged leader of the Sturm und Drang literary movement, Goethe set out on a journey to Italy to fulfil a personal and artistic quest and to find relief from his responsibilities and the agonies of unrequited love. As he travelled to Venice, Rome, Naples and Sicily he wrote many letters, which he later used as the basis for the Italian Journey. A journal full of fascinating observations on art and history, and the plants, landscape and the character of the local people....
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson notes that these works by Goethe share the same interest in his relationship with other remarkable minds.
Walter Pater cites Goethe's travelogue as a source for the observation about Raffaelle's painting of Saint Agatha.

book:28927881.description: Fausto, de Johann Wolfgang von Goethe es una obra tragica enteramente dialogada, concebida mas para ser leida que para ser representada (al estilo de La Celestina). Fue publicada en dos partes: Faust: der Tragodie erster Teil (Fausto: Primera parte de la tragedia) y Faust: der Tragodie zweiter Teil (Fausto: Segunda parte de la tragedia). Se trata de la obra mas famosa de Goethe y esta considerada como una de las grandes obras de la literatura universal. La figura del doctor Fausto, personaje legendario que....
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson describes the second part of Faust as a philosophy of literature and a product of Goethe's encyclopedic knowledge.
Walter Pater references Goethe's Faust to illustrate the union of Romantic spirit and Hellenism, specifically the character Euphorion.

Leo Tolstoy uses Goethe's Faust as an example of a work founded on borrowed elements, arguing that despite its qualities, it fails to produce a genuine artistic impression due to its lack of unity between form and content.
Matthew Arnold cites Swift's phrase 'sweetness and light' from the Battle of the Books as a key characterization of perfection.

book:web_493de26a.description: A lost play by the ancient Greek tragedian Sophocles, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies the source of a quotation as Sophocles' Œnomaus.

book:web_96d06011.description: Lost play by Sophocles, written circa 5th century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies a line as from Sophocles' lost play Inachus.

book:305549.description: Sophocles' Trachiniae is, in the editor's words, 'a subtle and sophisticated play about primitive emotions'. It is also a play which presents problems to a modern audience. Making full use of recent Sphoclean scholarship, Mrs Easterling attempts in her Introduction a detailed literary analysis of Trachiniae, helping the reader to understand better its intricate structure, the treatment of Deianira and Heracles, and the meaning of the final scenes. The notes in the Commentary of grammar, syntax and style inc...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes a line from Sophocles' play Trachiniæ.

book:web_d865d623.description: Posthumously published work on ethics by Jeremy Bentham, outlining his utilitarian moral philosophy, edited by John Bowring.
commentaries: Matthew Arnold refers to Bentham's 'Deontology' as a book, reading it to critique Bentham's ideas.

book:web_5fefb589.description: A book of the New Testament, an epistle written by Paul to the Christians in Rome, traditionally dated to around AD 57.
commentaries: Baruch Spinoza cites Paul's Epistle to the Romans to show that everyone can understand God's nature through the light of nature.

book:web_08ee8278.description: A travelogue and study of Mormonism, published anonymously as 'by One of Themselves' but actually written by the English journalist and historian William Hepworth Dixon.
commentaries: Matthew Arnold references Hepworth Dixon's book on the Mormons to illustrate a point about how people uncritically accept doctrines based on the number of followers or rifles.

book:web_c8fd8cee.description: A critical work by Samuel Taylor Coleridge exploring Greek classic poetry, based on his lectures and published posthumously.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references Coleridge's translation of a Homeric passage from his Introduction.

book:pg6081.description: Originally conceived as a short preface to Sibylline Leaves, by the time Coleridge's Biographia Literaria was published in 1817 it had expanded into a two-volume apologia for the Romantic poet's "literary life and opinions." Coleridge here develops a theory of the poetic imagination, in which an artist's passion, will, memory, and perception intersect to engender her or his work. This unique edition is essential to understanding the influences and ideology of Romanticism.

book:web_89aa67de.description: An unfinished philosophical work by Coleridge, announced in Biographia Literaria (1817) but never completed or published as a separate book. The reference is to a projected treatise within this work.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge references his own forthcoming work, Logosophia, where he plans to elaborate on the Dynamic Philosophy.

book:web_8af07ba9.description: A historical work by John Knox covering the Scottish Reformation.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle references Knox's History as a work that displays his drollery and true eye for the ridiculous.

book:816903.description: "Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains." The cry for human liberty sparked the French Revolution and questions the role of government in democracy. Includes two discourses. Origin of Inequalitythat inequality is the natural result of civilization. Political Economyexamines how politics affects people.
commentaries: Thomas Carlyle cites Rousseau's work 'contrat-social' as an example of his prophetic function.

book:web_55238b1c.description: A poem by Jean-Jacques Rousseau, often referred to as 'Ode to Fortune', written in the 18th century.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge reports that the person he is describing criticized Rousseau's poem for being more moralistic than lyrical.

book:84602.description: In On the Ideal Orator, (De oratore), Cicero, the greatest Roman orator and prosewriter of his day, gives his mature views on rhetoric, oratory, and philosophy. Cast in the lively, literary form of a dialogue, this classic work presents a daring view of the orator as the master of all language communication while still emphasizing his role at the heart of Roman society and politics. Cicero's conception of the ideal orator represents his own original synthesis of the positions of the philosophers and the rhe...
commentaries: Suetonius describes Cicero's dialogues on the perfect orator, which survive entire.

book:web_83002d30.description: A lost autobiographical poem in Greek by Cicero, recounting the events of his consulship in 63 BC.
commentaries: Suetonius describes Cicero's Greek commentary on his consulship, sent to Atticus and Posidonius.

book:web_0830bcb6.description: Cicero's Latin verse translation of Aratus's Greek poem 'Phaenomena', written in his youth.
commentaries: Suetonius describes Cicero's translation of Aratus' Phaenomena into Latin verse.

book:web_8833c554.description: A geographical treatise by the ancient Greek astronomer and mathematician Eudoxus of Cnidus, describing the known world and its regions.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Eudoxus' work 'Circuit of the World' to record a physician who advised constant exercise.

book:web_67afc06e.description: A lost geographical and ethnographic work by the Greek astronomer, mathematician, and geographer Eudoxus of Cnidus (c. 390–c. 340 BCE), describing peoples and customs of the known world.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Eudoxus' travelogue to describe the customs of the Massagetae.

book:web_a4003b17.description: A lost philosophical dialogue by Eudoxus of Cnidus, mentioned by Eratosthenes in his works addressed to Baton. Eudoxus was a Greek astronomer, mathematician, and philosopher, and this work is one of his lesser-known literary compositions.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions this work of Eudoxus as reported by Eratosthenes.

book:web_040aaffb.description: A poetic work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Empedocles, dealing with purification and reincarnation.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Empedocles' poem 'Purifications' as a source for his own origin.

book:web_e76b3261.description: A lost philosophical work by Xenocrates of Chalcedon, discussing the doctrines of Speusippus and Xenocrates himself, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: The subject wrote a book on the philosophy of Speusippus and Xenocrates.

book:web_1c0a8877.description: Lost historical memoirs by Aratus of Sicyon, a Greek statesman and general (271–213 BCE), cited by Plutarch in his Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch references Aratus's own commentaries to contradict a local religious tale about the battle, citing Aratus's account of the military action instead.
Plutarch cites Aratus's commentaries where he denies involvement in the attempt on the Piraeus, blaming Erginus instead.

book:19016323.description: Hesiod was an early Greek poet and rhapsode, who presumably lived around 700 BCE. His writings serve as a major source on Greek mythology, farming techniques, archaic Greek astronomy and ancient timekeeping. Of the many works attributed to Hesiod, three survive complete and many more in fragmentary state. They include Alexandrian papyri, some dating from as early as the 1st century BC, and manuscripts written from the eleventh century forward. He wrote a poem of some 800 verses, the Works and Days, which re...
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero states that Hesiod's Theogony contains these allegorical fables.
Marcus Tullius Cicero references Zeno's interpretation of Hesiod's Theogony, criticizing how it undermines established notions of the Gods.

book:27418.description: Hesiod, one of the oldest known Greek poets, stands out as the first personality in European literature. The Theogonycontains a systematic genealogy of the gods from the beginning of the world and an account of their violent struggles before the present order was established. The Works and Days, a compendium of moral and practical advice for a life of honest husbandry, throws a unique and fascinating light on archaic Greek society, ethics, and superstition. Hesiod's poetry is the oldest source for the myths...
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson identifies the source of the lines as a translation of Hesiod's 'Works and Days'.
Plutarch mentions Hesiod's famous work 'Works and Days' as an example of the kind of wisdom attributed to wise men of that era.

book:694475.description:
Hesiod describes himself as a Boeotian shepherd who heard the Muses call upon him to sing about the gods. His exact dates are unknown, but he has often been considered a younger contemporary of Homer. This volume of the new Loeb Classical Library edition offers a general introduction, a fluid translation facing an improved Greek text of Hesiod's two extant poems, and a generous selection of testimonia from a wide variety of ancient sources regarding Hesiod's life, works, and reception.
In "Theogony" Hesiod....
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes lines from Hesiod's Works and Days.

book:web_1d05e6e6.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher and poet Timon of Phlius, likely containing satirical or philosophical verses, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Images as a source for Timon's verse about Pyrrho.
Diogenes Laertius cites Timon's 'Images' to illustrate the Sceptic position on evident appearances.

book:web_46fa978d.description: Satirical poem by Timon of Phlius, lampooning various philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Timon's 'Silli' as praising Thales as an astronomer.
Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Silli to describe Socrates.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Timon's work 'Silli' as containing a critique of Pythagoras.
Diogenes Laertius quotes Timon's Silli as a source for Timon's verse about Pyrrho.
Diogenes Laertius mentions Timon as Diogenes Laertius of the Silli, a work of satirical poetry.

book:web_00005d7f.description: Ancient Greek satirical poems by Timon of Phlius, referenced in Plutarch's Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch mentions that Speusippus is described in Timon's work as good at a jest.

book:web_863a8fb5.description: A lost work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Democritus, referred to in Diogenes Laërtius' 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.' The text likely dealt with cosmology or atomic theory.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Democritus's own statement in his work 'Little World' regarding his age relative to Anaxagoras.

book:web_be13e2e8.description: A lost work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Democritus, known from ancient references such as Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Democritus recited his work 'The Great World' to the people as a defense against accusations of wasting his patrimony.

book:web_db4cc406.description: Lost work by the Greek philosopher Theophrastus, student of Aristotle, on the nature of happiness, critiqued by Cicero in 'Tusculan Disputations' for arguing that one cannot be happy under torture.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions Theophrastus's book 'a happy life' and notes that it is widely attacked.

book:web_91715cc1.description: A lost work by the Peripatetic philosopher Theophrastus, likely a dialogue or treatise featuring or discussing Callisthenes of Olynthus, the historian and nephew of Aristotle. Referenced by Cicero in Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero notes that Theophrastus's work 'Callisthenes' is criticized for a particular sentence.

book:web_c1614ca5.description: A lost work by Theophrastus, possibly a dialogue or treatise about the Megarian school of philosophy, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Theophrastus' work 'Megaric Philosopher' as a source for Diogenes' reaction to a mouse.

book:web_0cc4d64d.description: A treatise on minerals and stones by Theophrastus, a student of Aristotle, written circa 315 BCE. It is one of the earliest known works on mineralogy.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder notes that Theophrastus refers to this fable in his Treatise on Stones.

book:web_f546969f.description: A lost work by Theophrastus, a student of Aristotle, discussing ethics and character. The citation refers to an anecdote about Pericles.
commentaries: Plutarch cites Theophrastus's work 'Morals' as a source for an anecdote about Pericles' behavior during his illness.

book:web_469860e4.description: Lost work by Theophrastus on monarchy, referenced by Plutarch in Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch cites Theophrastus's work 'On Monarchy' for an anecdote about Themistocles at the Olympic games.

book:web_617eb27c.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Cleanthes (c. 330–c. 230 BCE), interpreting the philosophy of Heraclitus. Cleanthes succeeded Zeno as head of the Stoic school.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists Cleanthes' book, the Explanations of Heraclitus, among his works.

book:pg44125.description:

How Gyges took the kingdom from Candaules

Persian culture
History & geography....

book:web_4fe3bcea.description: A philosophical work by Crantor of Soli, a member of the early Academy, known for its consolation themes and referenced by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions Crantor's work 'Consolation' as containing a similar story.

book:web_1822bd1f.description: A lost Roman comedy by Caecilius Statius, quoted by Cicero in Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero quotes Statius's play 'Synephebi' as an example of human concern for posterity, which he uses to argue for the immortality of the soul.
Marcus Tullius Cicero quotes a line from Statius's play Synephebi to dramatize his appeal to the public regarding religion.

book:2104084.description: When first performed, The Eunuch was a great success. Today, with its larger-than-life characters (particularly the boastful soldier Thraso and the toady Gnatho), its farcical and exaggerated humour and its vigorous action, it strikes the modern reader as the funniest and most Plautine of Terence's six comedies.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero identifies a passage as being from Terence's play 'Eunuch'.

book:web_84e26db3.description: A philosophical dialogue on the ideal state and Roman politics, written by Cicero in the 1st century BC.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero quotes Scipio as speaking within the book 'Commonwealth', attributing the ideas to Scipio.

book:web_8a522b2d.description: A lost work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Zeno of Elea, discussing Pythagorean doctrines.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius lists 'one on the Doctrines of the Pythagoreans' among Zeno's works.

book:web_93a731cf.description: Lost work by the pre-Socratic philosopher Zeno of Elea, known for his paradoxes and dialectical arguments.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Zeno's own work, 'Conversations', to illustrate his style of writing.

book:web_8d439258.description: A lost philosophical work by Zeno of Elea, known only through references in later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's work to explain the mechanism of a solar eclipse.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's work to explain the cause of lightning.

book:web_6c6d6929.description: Lost historical work by Timaeus of Tauromenium, composed in the 3rd century BCE, covering the history of Sicily. Only fragments survive.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero cites Timaeus as a source for the description of Syracuse.

book:web_6577c538.description: A lost tragedy by Euripides, referenced in Cicero's Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references a play by Euripides to illustrate an opinion about death.

book:web_7f967e87.description: A lost tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Euripides, first performed circa 412 BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius describes Crantor quoting a line from Euripides' Andromeda to Arcesilaus.

book:web_ad93b68d.description: A tragedy by Euripides, also known as The Phoenician Women.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies a line as from Euripides' play Phœnissæ.

book:3036064.description: Euripides' powerful investigation of religious ecstasy and the resistance to it is an argument for moderation, rejecting the lures of pure reason as well as pure sensuality.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius identifies a line as coming from Euripides' Bacchae.
Plutarch describes a performance of Euripides' play at a banquet, where the head of Crassus is used as a prop.

book:1152977.description: Based on the conviction that only translators who write poetry themselves can properly recreate the celebrated and timeless tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, The Greek Tragedy in New Translations series offers new translations that go beyond the literal meaning of the Greek in order to evoke the poetry of the originals. Under the editorship of Herbert Golder and the late William Arrowsmith, each volume includes a critical introduction, commentary on the text, full stage directions, and a glo...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius states the line is taken from Euripides' play Orestes.
Diogenes Laertius identifies these lines as coming from Euripides' play Erestes.

book:web_d7686eb1.description: A lost tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Euripides, likely written in the late 5th century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes a parody of lines from Euripides' Antiope.

book:9726631.description:
Testo greco a fronte
Una delle tragedie greche piu famose e rappresentate. Il dramma di una amore assoluto che si trasforma, per il tradimento di Giasone, in feroce odio e desiderio di vendetta. Una vendetta che coinvolgera anche i figli che Medea ha avuto da Giasone.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Chrysippus quoted nearly the whole of Euripides's Medea in one of his writings.
Diogenes Laertius notes that a line in the text is from Euripides' play Medea.

book:web_2157e119.description: A lost tragedy by Euripides, quoted by Crantor in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Euripides' play 'Bellerophon' as cited by Crantor.

book:1374959.description: Based on the conviction that only translators who write poetry themselves can properly re-create the celebrated and timeless tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides, the Greek Tragedy in New Translations series offers new translations that go beyond the literal meaning of the Greek in order to evoke the poetry of the originals. Under the general editorship of Peter Burian and Alan Shapiro, each volume includes a critical introduction, commentary on the text, full stage directions, and a glossary of...
commentaries: Clitus quotes a line from Euripides's Andromache to taunt Alexander.

book:web_46983f93.description: A tragedy by the ancient Greek playwright Euripides, likely first performed around 423 BCE. It deals with the aftermath of the war of the Seven against Thebes.
commentaries: Plutarch references Euripides' play 'Suppliants' as a source for a story that is then contradicted by Aeschylus.

book:240068.description: "The Electra of Euripides has the distinction of being, perhaps, the best abused, and, one might add, not the best understood, of ancient tragedies. "A singular monument of poetical, or rather unpoetical perversity;" "the very worst of all his pieces;" are, for instance, the phrases applied to it by Schlegel. Considering that he judged it by the standards of conventional classicism, he could scarcely have arrived at any different conclusion. For it is essentially, and perhaps consciously, a protest against....
commentaries: Plutarch notes that a singer performing a chorus from Euripides's play moved the captains to compassion, preventing the destruction of Athens.

book:web_f5e315ee.description: Lost tragedy by Euripides, known only from fragments.
commentaries: Voltaire attributes the first written expression of the idea that one's fatherland is wherever one feels comfortable to Euripides, specifically in his play 'Phaeton'.

book:22104860.description: In this new translation of Euripides' celebrated Greek tragedy, W.S. Merwin and George E. Dimock, Jr. offer a compelling look at the devastating consequence of 'man's inhumanity to man.' A stern critique of Greek culture, Iphigeneia at Aulis condemns the Trojan War by depicting the power of political ambition and the ensuing repercussions of thoughtlessly falling to the will of constituency. The translation impressively re-creates the broad array of moral and emotional tones conveyed by Euripides, with a co...
commentaries: Voltaire cites Euripides as an example of an author who imitated Homer without being accused of plagiarism.

book:134893.description: Heir to the throne of Ephesus, Heraclitus gave up his kingdom and chose, instead of the trappings of power, to seek the word of wisdom. Twent-five hundred years before Einstein, Heraclitus declared that energy is the essence of matter, that everything becomes energy in flux, in relativity: "All things change to fire, /and fire exhausted/falls back into things". His great book, On Nature, the world's first coherent philosophical treatise, has been long lost to history -- but its surviving fragments have for....
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius refers to Heraclitus as Diogenes Laertius of a book on nature.

book:web_13a069ea.description: A lost work by the Peripatetic philosopher Dicæarchus of Messina, containing dialogues held at Mytilene arguing for the mortality of the soul.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero mentions Dicæarchus's three books 'Lesbiacs' arguing for the mortality of the soul.

book:web_63423a85.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Diogenes of Seleucia (Diogenes the Babylonian), who wrote on the allegorical interpretation of Athena's birth from Zeus. The text is known only through references in later authors such as Cicero.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero cites Diogenes the Babylonian's book 'A Treatise concerning Minerva', noting its content regarding the birth of Minerva.

book:web_6132e160.description: Lost work by the Stoic philosopher Diogenes of Seleucia (Diogenes the Babylonian), discussing the nature of voice and hearing.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Diogenes of Babylon's 'On the Voice' for the definition of voice.

book:web_61d26702.description: An epic poem by the Roman poet Gnaeus Naevius, composed around 235 BCE, recounting the First Punic War. It is one of the earliest works of Latin literature.
commentaries: Suetonius references Naevius's work 'Punic War'.

book:web_c881bbff.description: Lost work by Aristoxenus, a Peripatetic philosopher and music theorist, containing historical anecdotes about philosophers, including the story that Plato wished to burn all writings of Democritus.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristoxenus's work for the story that Plato wanted to burn Democritus's writings.

book:web_0eac6096.description: A biography of Plato written by the Peripatetic philosopher and music theorist Aristoxenus. The work is now lost but was cited by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Aristoxenus's work 'Life of Plato' is the source for the seventh Aristotle.

book:web_7aefe6df.description: Lost work by Aristoxenus, a 4th-century BC Greek philosopher and music theorist, detailing the life and circle of Pythagoras.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristoxenus' work for an account of Pherecydes' death and burial.

book:web_682ffa8c.description: A collection of iambic poems by the Hellenistic poet Callimachus, likely composed in the 3rd century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Callimachus' work for a different version of the tripod story, which Callimachus in turn attributes to Leander.

book:1313376.description:
Callimachus of Cyrene, 3rd century BCE, became after 284 a teacher of grammar and poetry at Alexandria. He was made a librarian in the new library there and prepared a catalogue of its books. He died about the year 240. Of his large published output, only 6 hymns, 63 epigrams, and fragments survive (the fragments are in Loeb no. "421"). The hymns are very learned and artificial in style; the epigrams are good (they are also in the Loeb Greek Anthology volumes).
Lycophron of Chalcis in Euboea was a contempor...
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes an epigram by Callimachus recounting Pittacus's advice on marriage.

book:web_70eadd48.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations. The work argued against Epicurean theology.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero cites Posidonius's observation that Epicurus's professed belief in the Gods was insincere, motivated by fear of public opinion.

book:web_c992f3de.description: A lost multi-book treatise by the Greek Stoic philosopher Posidonius, discussing celestial bodies. It is referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers' (c. 230 CE).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the seventh book of his treatise On the Heavenly Bodies stating the sun is pure fire.

book:web_6cbca3d6.description: A lost work on meteorology by the Greek Stoic philosopher Posidonius, written in the 1st century BCE.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in Meteorological Elements defining the world.

book:web_eb9c29f3.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, defining poetic expression as metrical or rhythmical diction. Referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (c. 230 CE).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius' definition of a poetical expression from his work on style.

book:web_764d7627.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius of Apamea, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Posidonius's second book on Natural Philosophy for the doctrine of active and passive principles.

book:web_c3493513.description: Lost treatise on ethics by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, cited by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius refers to Posidonius' first book on Ethics for a proof of the reality of virtue.

book:web_22a5a3c8.description: A work on natural philosophy by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius of Apamea, now lost, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the fifteenth book of his Discussions on Natural Philosophy stating the world is spherical.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the second book of his Discourses on Natural Philosophy regarding the vacuum.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the first book of his Discourses on Natural Philosophy affirming the world is one.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's work on natural philosophy to explain the nourishment of the sun, moon, and stars.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's work on natural philosophy to define snow.

book:web_f2b0d182.description: Lost work on natural philosophy by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the sixteenth book of his Disclosures on Natural Philosophy stating the sun is larger than the earth.

book:web_5e3eaba3.description: A treatise on the gods by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in the thirteenth book of his treatise On Gods discussing mind penetrating the world.
Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius in his treatise On Gods claiming the heaven as the dominant principle.

book:web_cda60d95.description: A now-lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, entitled 'Exhortations' (Protrepticus), referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that Posidonius' Exhortations agree that virtue may be taught.

book:web_7d84e5a8.description: A lost philosophical treatise on duties by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's statement that the wise man will pray.

book:web_4ad0e310.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, likely written in the 1st century BCE, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's Exhortatory Essays for the idea that one should not abandon philosophy due to differing opinions.

book:web_ed99a490.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher and polymath Posidonius, likely a treatise on astronomy or meteorology, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Posidonius's third book of Heavenly Phænomena for the denial of substantial reality to a superficies.

book:web_2835d2f9.description: A lost work on meteorology by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius of Apamea, cited by later authors such as Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's Meteorology for an explanation of the rainbow.

book:web_d8b0c5b7.description: A treatise on divination by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, now lost but referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's works on natural philosophy and divination to support the existence of divination.

book:web_0eb1a743.description: A philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius, now lost, discussing the concept of fate.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's work on Fate to support the doctrine of fate.

book:web_8d4037e9.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Posidonius discussing the criterion of truth.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Posidonius's 'On Criteria' for his opinion on right reason as a criterion.

book:web_56bbf1fb.description: Lost treatise on ancient luxury by the Cyrenaic philosopher Aristippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus' treatise to note Socrates' attachment to Alcibiades.

book:web_b194f611.description: A lost work by the Cyrenaic philosopher Aristippus (c. 435–356 BCE) that discusses natural philosophers, including Pythagoras.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus's work 'Account of Natural Philosophers' for an etymology of Pythagoras's name.

book:web_9b089814.description: Lost work by Aristippus of Cyrene (or possibly his grandson), cited by Diogenes Laërtius, containing anecdotes about ancient luxury.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius recounts a story from Aristippus's work about Periander's mother.

book:web_b894432d.description: A lost work by Aristippus the Younger (or possibly Aristippus of Cyrene), referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The treatise discussed anecdotes about ancient philosophers and their luxurious or amorous affairs.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus' work 'On Ancient Luxury' as stating that Xenocrates loved Polemo.
Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus for an anecdote about Aristotle's relationship with Hermias' concubine.
Diogenes Laertius cites Aristippus's treatise 'The Ancient Luxury' as the source for Theophrastus's attachment to Nicomachus.
