book:web_509c94fe.description: A lost work by the ancient Greek philosopher Antisthenes, founder of Cynicism, in which he discussed natural theology and the existence of many national gods and one natural deity. The work is cited by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references Antisthenes's book 'the Natural Philosopher' to criticize his view that there are many national gods and one natural God.

book:web_f7c86349.description: A lost polemical dialogue composed by Antisthenes against Plato, known only from later references.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius attributes a dialogue titled Sathon to Antisthenes, written against Plato.

book:web_1bc6789d.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher Antisthenes (c. 445–365 BCE), likely a historical or biographical account of philosophical schools and their founders, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Antisthenes' work 'Successions' to attribute the origin of the apophthegm 'know yourself' to Phemonoe.
Diogenes Laertius references Antisthenes' work Successions as supporting the account that Diogenes died by holding his breath.
Antisthenes' work 'Successions' is cited as evidence of Heraclitus' lofty spirit.
Diogenes Laertius cites Antisthenes's 'Successions' for a different account of Zeno's interrogation and speech.
Diogenes Laertius references Antisthenes's book as evidence for Democritus's travels to Egypt.

book:web_0a20a926.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, likely containing definitions of logical terms such as 'axiom'; referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus' 'Dialectic Definitions' for the definition of an axiom.

book:web_7f387161.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus in the first book of his treatise On the Physical Arts regarding the vacuum.

book:web_40cd3fda.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The treatise argued that certain things are not desirable as ends in themselves.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius notes that Chrysippus repeats a doctrine in this treatise.

book:web_3e00f02a.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, discussing political theory and the ideal state.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Chrysippus's treatise On Polity for the same doctrine of common women among the wise.

book:web_66ffb32e.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, likely discussing Zeno of Citium's technical terminology.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's treatise where he says only the wise are kings.

book:web_6a5d6761.description: Lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's Republic as attesting to the authorship of Zeno's Republic.

book:web_fbfad87d.description: A work on Stoic physics by Chrysippus, now lost but referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus in his Physics as also discussing the elements.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's Physics for the definition of Primary Matter as the substance of all existing things.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's 'Physics' (book 2) for the claim that voice is a body.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's 'Physics' (book 12) for the definition of the criterion of truth.

book:web_a0adfb65.description: A Stoic treatise by Chrysippus examining emotions as judgments, foundational to Stoic ethics.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's work on the Passions for the view that perturbations are judgments.

book:web_0867a37f.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers'.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's argument that all offences are equal.

book:web_4bc27c91.description: A lost treatise by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, cited by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The work consisted of at least twelve books and discussed the nature of the soul.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's 'On the Soul' (book 12) to define phantasia as an impression on the mind.

book:web_a0929c4e.description: A lost philosophical treatise by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus of Soli, written in the 3rd century BCE, discussing the nature and method of definition.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references both Antipater's and Chrysippus' works on definitions, with Chrysippus offering an alternative explanation.

book:web_0e1f3be8.description: A lost treatise by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, describing a thousand-line argument permitting the consumption of dead bodies.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius describes a shocking directive in Chrysippus's treatise on Justice.

book:web_5be8aa36.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes Chrysippus's treatise, which contains arguments about the wise man's provision for means.

book:web_1721568d.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. The original Greek title is likely Φυσικῶν ζητημάτων (Physikōn Zētēmatōn).
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Chrysippus's first book of Investigations in Natural Philosophy for the active and passive principles.

book:web_273b11f5.description: A lost treatise by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's 'On Reason' (book 1) for his view on criteria.

book:web_076e12e7.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, likely written in the 3rd century BCE, discussing divine providence and the governance of the world.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus in his works on Providence to support the idea that the world is governed by intellect.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus in the first book of his essay On Providence claiming the heaven as the dominant principle.
Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus in the first volume of his treatise On Providence affirming the world is an animal with reason.

book:web_28cafde2.description: A work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus on different ways of life, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers'.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's view that the wise man will take part in state affairs.
Diogenes Laertius references Chrysippus's first book On Lives for the same opinion about the wise man's love.

book:web_44fa9a26.description: A lost treatise by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, discussing the concept of the end or goal of life (telos). Referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's treatise 'on Ends' to support the statement about the first inclination of an animal.

book:web_076d1cc5.description: A Stoic philosophical work by Chrysippus, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, discussing ideal governance and controversial social norms.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Chrysippus's treatise on Polity contains controversial doctrines about marriage.

book:web_9b82909d.description: Lost work by Stoic philosopher Chrysippus discussing the concept of void or vacuum.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus in his essay On a Vacuum discussing the existence of a vacuum outside the world.

book:web_dea946e1.description: A lost work on logic and dialectic by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's work 'Dialectics' to define the combined proposition.

book:web_6e85c837.description: A lost treatise on ethics by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, originally part of a larger work. It is cited by Diogenes Laërtius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's first book on Virtues for the doctrine that virtue is sufficient for happiness.

book:web_48d2139d.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's treatise on Divination to support the universal existence of divination.

book:web_34108b91.description: Stoic philosopher, wrote a treatise on fate.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Chrysippus's treatise on Fate to support the doctrine that all things are produced by fate.

book:web_84c73f2a.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, discussing the Stoic concept of the highest good.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius refers to Chrysippus' explanation in his treatise on the Chief Good.

book:web_b232a6e0.description: A lost philosophical work by the Stoic philosopher Chrysippus, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius attributes the idea that virtues reciprocally follow one another to Chrysippus's treatise On Laws.

book:web_c9b38daf.description: A treatise on diseases by the Greek philosopher Heraclides of Pontus, referenced by Diogenes Laertius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Heraclides' medical treatise as a source for Empedocles' communication with Pausanias.

book:web_30f4d045.description: A famous speech by the Athenian orator Demosthenes, urging resistance against Philip II of Macedon, delivered around 341 BCE.
commentaries: Polybius references Demosthenes's 'Third Philippic' as a source.

book:4593395.description:
Thucydides' book is now entitled History of the Peloponnesian War. His entire contribution to history & historiography is contained in this dense history of the 27-year war between Athens & allies against Sparta & its allies. It breaks off near the end of the 21st year. Thucydides believed the war represented an event of unparalleled magnitude. He intended his account to serve as "a possession for all time."
Thucydides is regarded as one of the 1st true historians. Like his predecessor Herodotus, he places....
commentaries: Herodotus cites a passage from Thucydides as a parallel for the Greek phrase being discussed.

book:web_f48206f7.description: A lost work by Epicurus discussing the criterion of truth, also referred to as 'The Rule and Judgment of Things'.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero references Epicurus's volume 'the Rule and Judgment of Things' as the source for the reasoning about preconception.

book:web_60bf387b.description: A lost philosophical work by Epicurus, referenced by Cicero in his Tusculan Disputations, discussing Epicurean theology and the nature of the gods.
commentaries: Marcus Tullius Cicero notes that Epicurus wrote a book on sanctity, but dismisses it as a trifling work that allows the Gods in words while denying them in fact.
Marcus Tullius Cicero introduces the doctrines from Epicurus's first book on the Nature of the Gods.

book:web_a9e83b37.description: A lost work by the Hellenistic philosopher Epicurus, likely a treatise on his atomistic and ethical doctrines.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Epicurus's work 'Fundamental Principles' to attest to the virtue of Metrodorus.

book:web_de7ab949.description: Treatise by Epicurus on the ultimate end of life, arguing that pleasure is the highest good.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius quotes from Epicurus's treatise on the Chief Good to illustrate his hedonistic philosophy.

book:web_bdb8e1cc.description: Lost philosophical work by Epicurus, likely a dialogue on pleasure and friendship, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Epicurus's Banquet as a source for the statement that the wise man will never indulge in drunkenness.

book:web_7d6cf2f5.description: A major philosophical treatise by Epicurus, originally in 37 books, of which only fragments survive. The citation refers to the eleventh book.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius references Epicurus's treatise 'On Nature' (book 11) to support a statement about the size and brightness of celestial bodies.

book:web_e189c24f.description: A lost work by the Greek philosopher Alcidamas, mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius. It discusses natural philosophy and claims Zeno and Empedocles were pupils of Parmenides.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Alcidamas's work 'Natural Philosophy' as a source for the philosophical lineage of Zeno and Empedocles.

book:26252.description: Plotinus is the last great philosopher of antiquity, although in more than one respect, a precursor of modern times. The Enneadsbring together Neoplatonism--mystic passion and ideas from Greek philosophy--together with striking variants of the Trinity and other central Christian doctrines, to produce a highly original synthesis.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references a specific portion of Plotinus's Enneads.
Diogenes Laertius attributes the view that justice exists by nature to Chrysippus's treatise On the Beautiful.
Augustine describes reading the Psalms and being kindled towards God.

book:web_3b15caf6.description: First book of the Bible, traditionally attributed to Moses.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo reflects on the gift of writing given to Moses for the book of Genesis, wishing he had been given similar eloquence for the same task.

book:web_4b3bd7e6.description: First book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament, traditionally attributed to Moses, containing the creation narrative and early history of humanity.
commentaries: John Locke references Moses as the source of the biblical creation narrative, using the account to illustrate a point about measuring duration.

book:web_f9c9cf99.description: The first five books of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), traditionally attributed to Moses, composed around the 15th–13th century BCE.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references the Pentateuch as containing early mentions of linen and woolen fabrics, specifically citing Leviticus 13.

book:web_5d2c6e45.description: A prophetic book in the Hebrew Bible/Old Testament, attributed to the prophet Isaiah, traditionally dated to the 8th century BCE.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo notes that Ambrose recommended the book of Isaiah, and that he initially found it difficult.

book:web_d012299c.description: A treatise by Saint Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, written around 387 AD, discussing the patriarch Abraham as a model of faith and virtue.
commentaries: Voltaire cites St. Ambrose's work 'On Abraham' to show his materialist view of creation except for the Trinity.

book:web_f6c658f1.description: A lost work by the Stoic philosopher Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, which argued that the chief good is to live in accordance with nature. Referenced in Diogenes Laërtius' 'Lives of the Eminent Philosophers'.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius credits Zeno as the first to state that the chief good is to live according to nature, in his treatise on the Nature of Man.

book:web_1d7afdce.description: Lost work by Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius states that Zeno first divided philosophy into three parts in his treatise on Reason.

book:web_b6c61b23.description: Lost treatise by the Stoic philosopher Zeno of Citium, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's treatise On Essence for the principle of active and passive in the universe.

book:web_c6836a35.description: A lost work by the founder of Stoicism, Zeno of Citium, outlining his ideal state and controversial social doctrines.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions that Zeno denounced education in his Republic.
Diogenes Laertius references Zeno's Republic for the teaching that only the virtuous are true citizens.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's Republic and a poem for his teachings on community of women and other societal structures.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's statement that the wise man will marry and beget children.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's Republic for the doctrine that the wise man will love young men with aptitude for virtue.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno's Republic for the doctrine that women should be common among the wise.

book:web_f315e782.description: Lost work by Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, on the subject of love. Mentioned by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Zeno's work The Art of Love as containing discussions on amatory subjects.

book:web_e88e739c.description: A philosophical work by Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism, discussing the four kinds of perturbations: grief, fear, desire, and pleasure.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Zeno's work on the Passions as a source for the classification of perturbations.

book:web_3d19bc6e.description: Lost treatise by the Stoic philosopher Zeno of Citium, referenced by Diogenes Laërtius in Lives of the Eminent Philosophers.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno discussing the creation of the world from the elements in his treatise On the Universe.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno in his treatise On the Universe discussing the creation and destruction of the world.
Diogenes Laertius cites Zeno in his treatise On the Universe affirming the world is one.

book:web_01e81335.description: A lost encyclopedic work by Varro, divided into 41 books covering human and divine matters. It was a major source for later authors like Augustine.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo describes Varro's monumental work on Roman antiquities, detailing its structure and contents.

book:web_67ada1ed.description: Ancient Roman work on Roman religion, largely lost, cited by Augustine in The City of God.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo mentions Varro as a source for information about the religious efforts of King Numa.

book:web_08a7c8da.description: A work by the Roman scholar Varro, likely part of his lost 'Antiquitates rerum divinarum', discussing the hierarchy of gods. The citation refers to his classification of souls.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Varro's book on the select gods to explain his three grades of soul in universal nature.

book:web_e75e7a39.description: A treatise on the Latin language by the Roman scholar Varro, originally published around 43 BCE.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Varro's linguistic work as a source for the mother of the Lares.
James George Frazer cites Varro's work De lingua Latina as evidence that the full name Mamurius Veturius is preserved.
James George Frazer cites Varro's De lingua latina for an additional reference.
Pliny the Elder references Varro's work for the origin of the term 'Lucanian ox' for elephant.
Polybius references Varro's De Lingua Latina in a note about geographical divisions.
Suetonius mentions Varro's surviving treatise De Lingua Latina.

book:web_fd77041d.description: A treatise on agriculture written by the Roman scholar Varro, covering various aspects of farming and rural life.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Varro's explanation of the etymology of 'cuniculus'.
Pliny the Elder notes that the circumstance is not mentioned in Varro's extant works 'De Re Rusticâ' and 'De Linguâ Latinâ'.
Pliny the Elder notes that Varro and Columella have written extensively on this subject.
Pliny the Elder states that Pliny's remarks on hogs are likely derived from Varro's work.
Pliny the Elder cites Varro and Columella for a specific age recommendation for hogs.
Pliny the Elder cites Varro and Columella for a breeding recommendation for sows.
Pliny the Elder references Varro's statement about the timing of a hog's development and notes a scholarly debate.
Pliny the Elder notes that a saying about hogs is found in Varro's work.
Pliny the Elder cites Varro and Aulus Gellius for descriptions of Roman animal enclosures.

book:web_cf84c8b9.description: A historical treatise on English boroughs and their charters, written by the antiquary and historian Thomas Madox.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Madox's work as a source for information about adulterine guilds and fines paid to the king.
Adam Smith cites Madox's works to support the practice of farming town revenues to burghers.
Adam Smith again references Madox's work, along with Pfeffel, regarding jurisdictions granted to towns.

book:web_7918be44.description: A multi-volume history of New France (French colonies in North America) written by Jesuit historian Charlevoix, first published in 1744.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Charlevoix's history.
James George Frazer cites Charlevoix's history of New France.

book:web_d6b27036.description: A collection of tracts on the corn trade and corn laws, written by Charles Smith and referenced by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites the quantitative estimate of the average corn import from this work.

Adam Smith cites Adam Smith of the Tracts upon the Corn Trade as an authority on the effects of the corn bounty, noting his argument that the value of exported corn exceeds that of imported corn plus bounties.

book:web_5ba05e33.description: A historical and legal treatise on English poor laws, written by the English legal writer and clergyman Richard Burn.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Doctor Burn's work 'History of the Poor Laws' to discuss the hardship of certificate requirements.

book:550463.description:
Pliny the Elder, tireless researcher and writer, is author of the encyclopedic "Natural History," in 37 books, an unrivaled compendium of Roman knowledge.
The contents of the books are as follows. Book 1: table of contents of the others and of authorities; 2: mathematical and metrological survey of the universe; 3-6: geography and ethnography of the known world; 7: anthropology and the physiology of man; 8-11: zoology; 12-19: botany, agriculture, and horticulture; 20-27: plant products as used in medicine;....
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Pliny's Natural History as a source for the historical fact that the Romans used only copper money until shortly before the First Punic War.
Adam Smith cites Pliny's Natural History as a source for the early Roman use of unstamped copper bars as money.

book:web_4dce5d17.description: An encyclopedic work covering natural history, geography, medicine, and more, written by Pliny the Elder in the 1st century AD.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Pliny's Natural History as a source quoting the law.

book:550455.description: Pliny's Natural Historyis an astonishingly ambitious work that ranges from astronomy to art and from geography to zoology. Mingling acute observation with often wild speculation, it offers a fascinating view of the world as it was understood in the first century AD, whether describing the danger of diving for sponges, the first water-clock, or the use of asses' milk to remove wrinkles. Pliny himself died while investigating the volcanic eruption that destroyed Pompeii in AD 79, and the natural curiosity tha...
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Pliny's Natural History as an example of the superstitions about menstruation among civilized nations.
James George Frazer cites Pliny's Natural History, Ovid's Metamorphoses and Fasti, and Mannhardt's work.
James George Frazer cites Pliny's Natural History as a source on the mistletoe plant.
James George Frazer cites Pliny as the historical source that the Druids cut mistletoe in June.
James George Frazer notes that Pliny repeats a story previously attributed to Aelian.
James George Frazer cites Aelian's work on animals.
Suetonius cites Pliny's Natural History as a source for the description of the properties of satyrion, used in love-potions.
Suetonius notes Pliny the Elder was at the height of his reputation and favored by Vespasian, and credits him as an influence on the emperor's patronage of literature.
Suetonius mentions Pliny the Elder as a victim of the Vesuvius eruption, referencing his status as a naturalist and author of the Natural History.
Suetonius describes the Natural History as Pliny the Elder's principal surviving work, summarizing its structure and significance.
Suetonius identifies Pliny the Elder as Suetonius of the Natural History, distinguishing him from his nephew.

book:pg60230.description: A landmark in reference publishing and overseen and authenticated by the Smithsonian Institution's National Museum of Natural History, Natural Historypresents an unrivaled visual survey of Earth's natural history. Giving a clear overview of the classification of our natural world-over 6,000 species-Natural Historylooks at every kingdom of life, from bacteria, minerals, and rocks to fossils to plants and animals. Featuring a remarkable array of specially commissioned photographs, Natural Historylooks at thou...

book:web_4b5fefdb.description: A pamphlet proposing a scheme for poor relief by Sir Matthew Hale, likely published posthumously.
commentaries: Smith references Hales's computation of a labourer's family expenses and notes that Hales researched the subject carefully.

book:web_aa7a1c40.description: A work on the wool trade by the Reverend John Smith, referenced by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites John Smith's work to support the claim that English wool prices are depressed below those of inferior wool in Amsterdam.

book:web_5117a7c6.description: A biography of Julius Caesar included in Suetonius's collection 'De vita Caesarum' (Lives of the Caesars), written around 121 AD.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references Suetonius's account of Caesar's claim of descent from Venus.

book:web_e74103cf.description: A biography of Julius Caesar by the Roman historian Suetonius, part of his work 'De Vita Caesarum' (The Twelve Caesars), written around AD 121.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Suetonius's biography of Julius Caesar as the source for an account.

book:web_2556dd54.description: A biography of the Roman emperor Augustus, part of Suetonius's work 'De Vita Caesarum' (The Lives of the Caesars), written around AD 121.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Suetonius's 'Life of Augustus' as a source for the date of the secular games.
Pliny the Elder references Suetonius's work for a custom involving elephants and money.
Pliny the Elder references Suetonius's Life of Augustus as a source.

book:pg6400.description: Suetonius wrote his Lives of the Twelve Caesarsin the reign of Vespasian around A.D. 70. He conicled the extraordinary careers of Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula, Claudius, Nero, Vespasian and Domitian and the rest in technicolour terms. They presented some high and low times at the heart of the Roman Empire. The accounts provide us with perspicacious insights into the men as much as their reigns - and it was from Suetonius that subsequent writers such as Robert Graves drew so much of their material.

book:web_777a1ae0.description: A philosophical work by Thomas Hobbes, part of his 'Elements of Philosophy' series, first published in Latin in 1658.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge mentions Hobbes's 'De Natura Humana' as being preceded by Des Cartes's 'De Methodo'.

book:6359076.description:
Thomas Hobbes took a new look at the ways in which society should function, and he ended up formulating the concept of political science. His crowning achievement, Leviathan,remains among the greatest works in the history of ideas. Written during a moment in English history when the political and social structures as well as methods of science were in flux and open to interpretation, Leviathanplayed an essential role in the development of the modern world.
An outspoken royalist, Hobbes fled to France during...
commentaries: David Hume uses Hobbes's Leviathan as a comparison point for hypothetical uniform characters that would be disbelieved by a traveler.

book:web_97977356.description: A historical account of Massachusetts Bay Colony by Colonial Governor Thomas Hutchinson, originally published in multiple volumes. Volume 2 was published in 1767.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Hutchinson's History of Massachusetts Bay as a source for the fact that the colony paid off most of its public debts with a tenth of the original value of its paper money.

book:web_186dc1cb.description: A critical examination of Du Tot's economic treatise, published in 1740.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Mr Du Verney's book as a clear explanation of the Mississippi scheme's operations.

book:web_42706606.description: A work by the French physiocrat Pierre-Paul Mercier de la Rivière, originally published in 1767 as 'L'Ordre naturel et essentiel des sociétés politiques.'
commentaries: Adam Smith cites this book as the clearest exposition of the Economists' doctrine.

book:21331.description: A timeless collection of 80 of Aesop's best-loved fables--punctuated by the age-old morals that have instructed countless generations. This volume highlights such fables as "The Goose Who Laid the Golden Eggs," "The Mouse and the Frog," and the one and only "The Tortoise and the Hare."
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson cites Aesop's Fables as an example of a book that is not the work of a single author but of collective tradition.
Arthur Schopenhauer references Aesop's fables as a book given to children for educational purposes, noting the children's rationalist rejection of it.

book:web_c95a675b.description: A foundational work of mercantilist economic theory, published posthumously in 1664, arguing that a nation's wealth is measured by its stock of precious metals and advocating for a positive balance of trade.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Mun's book as a work whose title became a fundamental maxim in political economy.

book:web_db6cbe64.description: A book on commerce by Mr. Meggens, with a postscript added in 1756 correcting errors.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Mr Meggens' book 'Universal Merchant' and its postscript as a source for data on the annual importation of precious metals into Spain and Portugal.

book:web_eb9236d3.description: Historical work covering the Holy Roman Empire, including events under Frederick II and the Hohenstaufen dynasty.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Pfeffel's work on remarkable events under Frederick II and his successors.

book:pg10827.description: Few figures in intellectual history have proved as notorious and ambiguous as Niccolo Machiavelli. But while his treatise The Princemade his name synonymous with autocratic ruthlessness and cynical manipulation, The Discourses(c. 1517) shows a radically different outlook on the world of politics.In this carefully argued commentary on Livy's history of republican Rome, Machiavelli proposed a system of government that would uphold civic freedom and security by instilling the virtues of active citizenship, and...

book:780638.description: Purchase one of 1st World Library's Classic Books and help support our free internet library of downloadable eBooks. Visit us online at www.1stWorldLibrary.ORG- - Nicolo Machiavelli was born at Florence on 3rd May 1469. He was the second son of Bernardo di Nicolo Machiavelli, a lawyer of some repute, and of Bartolo-mmea di Stefano Nelli, his wife. Both parents were members of the old Florentine nobility. His life falls naturally into three periods, each of which singularly enough constitutes a distinct and....
commentaries: Niccolò Machiavelli references his own earlier work as a source for the methods used by the Romans.
Niccolò Machiavelli references his own earlier work, 'The Prince', as having already discussed the topic of whether princes should keep promises made under compulsion.

book:web_ac85aa5d.description: Travelogue by Pierre Poivre recounting his journeys and observations in Asia, particularly Cochin China and other regions.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Mr Poivre's observations on the price of sugar in Cochin China.

book:2279651.description:
Columella (Lucius Iunius Moderatus) of Gades (Cadiz) lived in the reigns of the first emperors to about 70 CE. He moved early in life to Italy where he owned farms and lived near Rome. It is probable that he did military service in Syria and Cilicia and that he died at Tarentum.
Columella's "On Agriculture" ("De Re Rustica") is the most comprehensive, systematic and detailed of Roman agricultural works. Book I covers choice of farming site; water supply; buildings; staff. II: Ploughing; fertilising; care of...
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Columella's agricultural work to explain Roman sowing practices.
Pliny the Elder cites Columella's agricultural treatise for advice on treating a disease in hogs.
Pliny the Elder cites Columella alongside Aristotle as a source for a surgical procedure on hogs.
Adam Smith cites Kalm's observations on North American colonial husbandry as evidence for a system of agriculture similar to that in Scotland.

book:web_1d9a744e.description: A treatise on historiography by the ancient Greek satirist and rhetorician Lucian, written in the 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Polybius references Lucian's work on how to write history.

book:web_4ea684a8.description: A monumental medieval Latin glossary, often referred to as Du Cange's Glossary, first published in 1678, with later editions including the Benedictine edition.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Du Cange's glossary as a source for the account of King John of France's coin adulteration.

book:web_782d3107.description: A treatise on economics proposing the use of paper money backed by land, written by Scottish economist John Law.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Mr Law's own discourse as explaining the principles of his project.

book:2455.description: A key figure in the development of Western literature, the Greek poet Theocritus of Syracuse, was the inventor of "bucolic" or pastoral poetry in the first half of the third century BC. These vignettes of country life, which center on competitions of song and love are the foundational poems of the western pastoral tradition. They were the principal model for Virgil in the Eclogues and their influence can be seen in the work of Petrarch and Milton. Although it is the pastoral poems for which he is chiefly fa...
commentaries: Adam Smith references Theocritus and his work Idyllium xxi to illustrate the historical poverty of fishermen.

book:web_565ee344.description: A comprehensive historical account of commerce by the Scottish economist and agriculturalist James Anderson, first published in 1764.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites Anderson's work to support a critical assessment of the Hudson's Bay Company's profits, noting that Anderson's analysis of Dobbs' accounts shows the profits were not extraordinary.

book:38262.description:
The Fortunes & Misfortunes of the Famous Moll Flanders (aka Moll Flanders) is a novel by Daniel Defoe, 1st published in 1722. It purports to be the true account of the life of the eponymous Moll, detailing her exploits from birth until old age.
By 1721, Defoe had become a recognised novelist, with the success of Robinson Crusoe in 1719. His political work was tapering off at this point, due to the fall of both Whig & Tory party leaders with whom he had been associated; Robert Walpole was beginning his rise....
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites De Foe's works as examples of novels meant to pass for histories, in contrast to Fielding's novels.

book:web_88fc1f85.description: An early economic treatise on grain policy, addressing regulation and trade of grain in France.
commentaries: Adam Smith references the 'elegant author' of the 'Essay on the Policy of Grain' as an observer of the decline in grain prices in France.

book:1479156.description: What is known? And how do we come to know it? These are the primary points of focus for metaphysics and epistemology, respectively. Here, in one of the classic works of early-modern empiricist philosophy, John Locke (1632-1704) attempts to answer these basic human questions by moving away from the rationalist notion of innate ideas to establish the concept of the tabula rasa in which the mind is initially impressed with ideas through perception of the external world of substance. The formation of basic idea...
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge critiques the first book of Locke's Essay, arguing it involves a logical fallacy.
Ralph Waldo Emerson mentions John Locke and his best-known work, noting that Locke's work combated Descartes' theory of innate ideas.
David Hume references Locke's chapter on power as a source for a popular explication of the idea of power and efficacy.
Voltaire quotes Locke's work to show his modest and religious opinion on the possibility of matter thinking, and notes the quarrels Locke faced for this view.
Voltaire references Locke's admission about sleep and thought, and notes that a French philosopher suffered persecution for agreeing with Locke.
Voltaire cites Locke's analysis to argue that the concept of free will is absurd, paraphrasing his demonstration that liberty is not a property of the will.

book:251510.description:
Plutarch (c. 45 -120 CE) wrote on many subjects. His forty-six Parallel Lives are biographies planned to be ethical examples in pairs, one Greek figure and one similar Roman, though the last four lives are single. They not only record careers and illustrious deeds but also offer rounded portraits of statesmen, orators, and military leaders.
Volume 1 contains:
Theseus
Romulus
Comparison of Theseus and Romulus
Lycurgus
Numa
Comparison of Lycurgus and Numa
Solon
Publicola
Comparison of Solon and Publicola
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Plutarch's Life of Numa.
James George Frazer cites Plutarch's Life of Numa as a source that preserves the full name Mamurius Veturius.
James George Frazer cites Plutarch's Life of Numa (along with Livy and Dionysius) as a source on the Salii.
Pliny the Elder notes that the subject is treated more extensively by Plutarch in this specific biography.

book:web_61c59d69.description: One of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, a biography of Cato (either Cato the Elder or Cato the Younger), written around the late 1st to early 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Plutarch's Life of Cato.

book:web_e4be2733.description: A doxographical work attributed to Plutarch, summarizing the philosophical opinions of various Greek schools, part of the Moralia.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Plutarch's work as a source for the opinions of earlier philosophers.

book:26929868.description:
Excerpt from Plutarch's Morals, Vol. 3: Translated From the Greek by Several Hands
It is sure, he that said it had no mind to live concealed, for he spoke it out of a design of being taken notice of for his very saying it, as if he saw deeper into things than every vulgar eye, and of purchasing to himself a reputation, how unjustly soever, by inveigling others into obscurity and retirement. But the poet says right:
I hate the man who makes pretence to wit,
Yet in his own concerns waives using it.
For they t...
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson cites Plutarch's 'Morals' as providing an alternative account of an anecdote about Scipio.

book:780477.description: Plutarch's Parallel Lives,written at the beginning of the second century A.D., form a brilliant social history of the ancient world. They were originally presented in a series of books that gave an account of one Greek and one Roman life, followed by a comparison of the two: Theseus and Romulus, Alcibiades and Coriolanus, Demosthenes and Cicero, Demetrius and Antony. Plutarch was interested in the personalities of his subjects and on the way their characters molded their actions, leading them to tragedy or....
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson identifies Plutarch as the key historian of heroism, praising his 'Lives' for refuting despondency and cowardice, and noting the wild courage and Stoicism in its anecdotes.
Ralph Waldo Emerson notes that Shakespeare and earlier dramatists used Plutarch's 'Lives' as a source for dramatic material.

book:3679100.description: Plutarch's Parallel Lives is a series of biographies, arranged in pairs illuminating virtues & vices. Surviving Lives contain 23 pairs, each with a Greek & a Roman Life, & 4 unpaired Lives. As explained in the opening of his Life of Alexander, he wasn't concerned with history so much as the influence of character on life & destiny. Whereas sometimes he barely touched on great events, he devoted much space to anecdote & incidental triviality, this often telling more about his subjects than their famous accom...
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson references a book titled 'Modern Plutarch' as a hypothetical source of standardized biographies that could arbitrarily fit any poet.
Plutarch quotes Zeno's aphorism about philosophical speech as a comparison to Phocion's concise style.

book:web_68c172bb.description: A collection of dialogues on various topics, part of Plutarch's Moralia, also known as Table Talk.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Plutarch's work in a footnote reference.
James George Frazer cites Plutarch's text on Isis and Osiris.
James George Frazer cites Plutarch's treatise on Isis and Osiris.

book:web_614ec6d6.description: A biography of the Roman general Lucullus, part of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, written around 75 AD.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Plutarch's work 'Lucullus' as the source for the anecdote about Cyzicus substituting a dough cow for a real one during a siege.

book:web_a871fc61.description: A doxographical work summarizing the views of various Greek philosophers on natural philosophy, often attributed to Plutarch.
commentaries: Diogenes Laertius mentions Casaubon referencing Plutarch's work to clarify a passage.

book:398122.description:
In 336 b.c. Philip of Macedonia was assassinated and his twenty-year-old son, Alexander, inherited his kingdom. Immediately quelling rebellion, Alexander extended his father's empire through-out the Middle East and into parts of Asia, fulfilling the soothsayer Aristander's prediction that the new king "should perform acts so important and glorious as would make the poets and musicians of future ages labour and sweat to describe and celebrate him."
The Life of Alexander the Greatis one of the first surviving...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references Plutarch's biography of Alexander as a source for the story of the horse Bucephalus.

book:web_f920f752.description: A philosophical treatise by Plutarch on the daimonion (divine sign) of Socrates, likely written in the late 1st or early 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder cites Plutarch's work 'De Deo Socratis' as giving a similar account of Hermotinus.

book:web_e52d47e9.description: A work by Plutarch, part of his Moralia, discussing the intelligence and instincts of animals. Originally written in Greek around the 1st century AD.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder mentions Plutarch's treatise in relation to the torpedo fish.

book:web_3836d4c2.description: A treatise by Plutarch, part of his Moralia, discussing the intelligence and behavior of animals.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references Plutarch's treatise for a statement about the whiteness of elephant teeth.

book:pg674.description:
If Jen can't get back to her usual self, she'll end up having to do everything all over again. Jen is a thirty-seven-year-old middle-school teacher in 2012. Overweight, underpaid, in debt, and with a bitter divorce pending, Jen wants to start over.
Then Jen is hit by a car. When she awakens, she is a thirteen-year-old kid with her same parents and siblings, but it is still 2012. Initially Jen resists accepting her new reality, insisting that she is thirty-seven years old. However, faced with the possibility...

book:web_a12cb55c.description: Biography of Roman general Sulla (Sylla) by Plutarch, part of his Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Plutarch references his own work on Sylla for further details.

book:web_eea45085.description: A biography of Dion of Syracuse, part of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, written around 75 CE.
commentaries: Plutarch references his own prior work for a more detailed account.

book:web_4180229f.description: Ancient Greek collection of biographies comparing famous Greeks and Romans, written by Plutarch around 100 AD.
commentaries: Plutarch presents Callimedon as a persecutor of free states, speaking against Phocion's plea to Antipater.

book:web_e6aca494.description: A biography of the Roman general and statesman Pompey the Great, part of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, written in the late 1st to early 2nd century AD.
commentaries: Plutarch refers to his own 'Life of Pompey' as the source for the subsequent story of Pompey's fate.

book:287515.description:
Plutarch (Plutarchus), ca. 45-120 CE, was born at Chaeronea in Boeotia in central Greece, studied philosophy at Athens, and, after coming to Rome as a teacher in philosophy, was given consular rank by the emperor Trajan and a procuratorship in Greece by Hadrian. He was married and the father of one daughter and four sons. He appears as a man of kindly character and independent thought, studious and learned.
Plutarch wrote on many subjects. Most popular have always been the 46 "Parallel Lives," biographies p...
commentaries: Polybius references Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes for the capture of Mantinea.
Polybius cites Plutarch's Life of Cleomenes regarding Cleomenes' project to restore the ancient constitution.

book:web_2e050acc.description: Biography of the Roman general and statesman Marcus Furius Camillus, part of Plutarch's Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Polybius references Plutarch's work 'Camillus' as a source for the account of the Gauls.

book:web_3175a97d.description: A biography of the Spartan general Lysander, part of Plutarch's Parallel Lives, written circa 100 AD.
commentaries: Polybius references Plutarch's work 'Lysander' as a source.

book:383568.description:
Plutarch (Plutarchus), ca. 45-120 CE, was born at Chaeronea in Boeotia in central Greece, studied philosophy at Athens, and, after coming to Rome as a teacher in philosophy, was given consular rank by the emperor Trajan and a procuratorship in Greece by Hadrian. He was married and the father of one daughter and four sons. He appears as a man of kindly character and independent thought, studious and learned.
Plutarch wrote on many subjects. Most popular have always been the 46 "Parallel Lives," biographies p...

Polybius cites Plutarch's Life of Aratus for details of Aratus' early exploits.

book:web_b3b482bf.description: Biography of the Athenian general Nicias, part of Plutarch's Parallel Lives.
commentaries: Polybius references Plutarch's work 'Nicias' as a source.
Polybius references Plutarch's Life of Nicias as a source for the office of the Polemarch.

book:web_54be81b5.description: An essay by the ancient Greek philosopher and biographer Plutarch, part of his Moralia collection, discussing the nature and dangers of superstition.
commentaries: Voltaire references Plutarch's essay 'Of Superstition' in a footnote, using it as a source against superstition.

book:web_48bd4b9e.description: A historical work by Robert Brady (c. 1627–1700), an English historian and physician, originally published in 1690. It discusses the history and legal status of English cities and boroughs.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Brady's work as a source for imperfect accounts from Doomsday-book regarding taxes paid by burghers.

book:web_6c9a8a92.description: A historical account of British public revenue, referenced by Adam Smith in The Wealth of Nations.
commentaries: Adam Smith cites this work as a source for the figures on public debt accumulation.

book:web_f71b9442.description: A philosophical and historical work by Scottish philosopher and judge Henry Home, Lord Kames.
commentaries: Adam Smith references Lord Kames' work as a source for a point about smuggling penalties.

book:334585.description: Livy's "Early History of Rome" tells of a small monarchical state's struggle to survive. It tells the story of the overthrow of the kings and the development of the Roman Republic. It depicts the qualities that allowed the early Romans to overcome internal disputes and foreign enemies and to recover after the nearly total destruction of their city in 390 BC. Livy writes with fairness, humanity, and an irresistible enthusiasm for the courage, honesty, and self-sacrifice that exemplified what it was to be Rom...
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references Livy's account of the restoration of old customs.
Niccolò Machiavelli cites Livy's historical observation on the Roman people's judgment, using it to support his argument about general versus particular judgment.
Niccolò Machiavelli again quotes Livy to highlight the admirable qualities of the Roman people in making their choices.
Plutarch references Livy's account of the battle to note a discrepancy in the reported victory and slaughter.

Its collections include around 14 million books, along with subst...
commentaries: Niccolò Machiavelli quotes Livy's work to support his argument about the role of religion in Roman politics.

book:web_abf9bbb1.description: An epitome of Livy's monumental history of Rome, 'Ab Urbe Condita', covering the city's founding to the early Empire.
commentaries: Polybius cites Livy's Epitome as a source clarifying the historical events.
Polybius cites Livy's Epitome for the number of Romans and Latins.

book:422880.description: Establishing the laws of universal gravity and the fundamental laws of motion, Newton's momentous 1687 essay stands as one of the most important works in physics, and it revolutionized the way scientists investigate and prove their theories. In Principia, Newton used mathematical terms to present the principles of time, force, and motion, which have been instrumental in the development of modern physics. In his introduction, the famed physicist and bestselling author Stephen Hawking shows how his work built...
commentaries: Ralph Waldo Emerson notes that Newton published his seminal work, the 'Principia,' in the year Swedenborg was born, establishing the theory of universal gravity.

book:9768108.description: Newton went to University to show that God exists. In this work, he presents biblical prophecies and study about them. According to him, Bible prophecy would not be understood "until the time of the end," which should be in the 21st century.
commentaries: Voltaire cites Newton's commentary on the Apocalypse as an example of a great genius having false judgment on a particular subject.

book:1230215.description: Benedict de Spinoza lived a life of blameless simplicity as a lens-grinder in Holland. And yet in his lifetime he was expelled from the Jewish community in Amsterdam as a heretic, and after his death his works were first banned by the Christian authorities as atheistic, then hailed by humanists as the gospel of Pantheism. His Ethics Demonstrated in Geometrical Order shows us the reality behind this enigmatic figure. First published by his friends after his premature death at the age of forty-four, the Ethic...
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge expresses a wish that the recommended theological texts contained passages as thoroughly Pauline and accordant with the Church's doctrines as the concluding page of Spinoza's Ethics, quoting from it.
Samuel Taylor Coleridge mentions Spinoza's Ethics as a possible example of a system that could be converted into irreligious Pantheism.

book:pg3800.description: The Nicomachean Ethics is a name normally given to Aristotle's best known work on ethics. The English version of the title derives from Greek Ethika Nikomakheia, transliterated Ethika Nikomacheia, which is sometimes also given in the genitive form as Ethikon Nikomakheion, Ethikon Nikomacheion. The Latin translations are Ethica Nicomachea or De Moribus ad Nicomachum. The work, which plays a preeminent role in defining Aristotelian ethics, consists of 10 books, originally separate scrolls, & is understood to....

book:36000554.description: Written by the Dutch philosopher Baruch Spinoza, the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus or Theologico-Political Treatise was one of the most controversial texts of the early modern period. It was a preemptive defense of Spinoza's later work, Ethics, published posthumously in 1677, for which he anticipated harsh criticism. The treatise was published anonymously in 1670 by Jan Rieuwertsz in Amsterdam. In order to protect the author and publisher from political retribution, the title page identified the city of pu...
commentaries: Baruch Spinoza references the Bible as a source for the term 'Glory' to describe love or blessedness.

book:6474210.description: Descartes' Discourse marks a watershed in European thought; in it, the author sets out in brief his radical new philosophy, which begins with a proof of the existence of the self (the famous "cogito ergo sum"). Next he deduces from it the existence and nature of God, and ends by offering a radical new account of the physical world and of human and animal nature. Written in everyday language and meant to be read by common people of the day, it swept away all previous philosophical traditions
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge cites Des Cartes's 'De Methodo' as having anticipated Hobbes's 'De Natura Humana'.

book:web_c228a0a6.description: A seminal work by Jesuit missionary José de Acosta, first published in Spanish in 1590, covering the natural history, geography, and indigenous cultures of the New World.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Acosta's work as a source describing a Mexican festival.

book:web_8819d01a.description: A natural and moral history of the Indies, originally published in Spanish as 'Historia natural y moral de las Indias'.
commentaries: James George Frazer cites Acosta's history as a source for Mexican sacrificial customs.

book:1569.description: This is an English translation of Aristophanes' famous comedy, Clouds, noted for its critique of philosophy, society and education. It includes essays on Old Comedy and the Theater of Dionysus, suggestions for further reading, notes on production, and a map. Focus Classical Library provides close translations with notes and essays to provide access to understanding Greek culture.
commentaries: The editor references Aristophanes' play 'Clouds' as an example of Socrates being depicted as a natural philosopher.
Plutarch quotes Aristophanes' play 'Birds' to mock Nicias' cowardice in resigning his command.

book:web_42fadc19.description: A work by Bernardino Telesio (Bernardinus Telesius) that critiques Aristotelian natural philosophy and proposes a new system based on principles derived from nature itself.
commentaries: The editor notes that Telesius wrote a work combating the Aristotelian system, titled 'De Rerum Natura juxta propria principia'.

book:web_11b32674.description: Neoplatonic philosopher; author of Platonic Theology, a systematic exposition of Plato's theology.
commentaries: Samuel Taylor Coleridge lists the early study of Plato and others as having prepared his mind for a certain philosophy.

Brown, Italo Calvino, Frederick Ahl, and Diane Middle...

Pliny the Elder cites Ovid's Fasti as a source of information about the deity Sangus.

Suetonius describes Ovid's Fasti as a work on Roman festivals, regretting that only part of it survives.

book:web_2214edea.description: A Latin elegiac poem consoling Livia on the death of her son Drusus, traditionally attributed to Ovid but sometimes to Pedo Albinovanus.
commentaries: Pliny the Elder mentions Pedo Albinovanus as a possible author of a consolation poem.

book:12745007.description: The celebrated Amores, comprising the four poems The Loves, The Art of Beauty, The Remedies for Love, and The Art of Love are the product of Ovid's late youth and jaunty middle age. In these verses, not only do we hear the passionate voice of one of the most talented poets of antiquity, but we can perceive the hum and stir of the Roman streets, the crowds in the fashionable walks, the light of parties at evening, the theaters, the races, the shops, and the chatter in the boudoirs. Taken together, these poem...
commentaries: Pliny the Elder references Ovid's work on the use of eggs in purification rituals.
Suetonius mentions Ovid's Ars Amandi as a love elegy with passionate and luscious descriptions.

book:3077838.description: Ovid's "Amores" translated by Guy Lee in the 1960s.
commentaries: Baruch Spinoza quotes Ovid's Amores to illustrate the idea that lovers share hopes and fears, and that it is unnatural to love what another rejects.
Baruch Spinoza notes that Spinoza transposes verses from Ovid's Amores.

book:20738843.description:
This is an alternate cover edition for ISBN13: 9780140423556
In the twenty-one poems of the "Heroides", Ovid gave voice to the heroines and heroes of epic and myth. These deeply moving literary epistles reveal the happiness and torment of love, as the writers tell of their pain at separation, forgiveness of infidelity or anger at betrayal. book:web_cf16db80.description: A foundational work on the philosophy of science by William Whewell, first published in 1840 in two volumes.
commentaries: Francis Bacon cites Whewell's book as one of two authorities that criticize Bacon's classification of prerogative instances.

book:web_939f3edf.description: One of the Bridgewater Treatises, examining astronomy and physics in relation to natural theology.
commentaries: Charles Darwin quotes Whewell's Bridgewater Treatise as an epigraph.

book:web_ea10c99d.description: A foundational work on the philosophy of science by William Whewell, originally published in 1840, which argues for the role of ideas and inductive reasoning in scientific discovery.
commentaries: Herbert Spencer references Whewell's companion work as providing further evidence for the indefiniteness of early science.
Herbert Spencer quotes Whewell's work to support the claim that primitive science was indefinite.

book:web_2fab096d.description: Foundational multi-volume work on human physiology by Swiss anatomist and physiologist Albrecht von Haller, published between 1757 and 1766.
commentaries: The editor cites Haller's work in physiology as having thoroughly covered the subject.

book:web_6c46c945.description: A work of natural philosophy by the Roman Stoic philosopher Seneca the Younger, covering topics such as meteorology, earthquakes, and other natural phenomena.
commentaries: Francis Bacon compares Seneca's clearer statement of an opinion in his Natural Philosophy to those of Ovid and Bacon.

book:32938676.description:
The Stoic writings of the philosopher Seneca offer powerful insights into the art of living, the importance of reason and morality, and continue to provide profound guidance to many through their eloquence, lucidity and timeless wisdom.

"Sometimes even to live is an act of courage."
Seneca composed the Consolations while in exile on Corsica during 40-44 AD and used each opportunity to show off in writing his trendy Stoic ideas about life and the universe. book:web_d5aa9e95.description: Foundational work on magnetism and electricity, published in 1600.

book:pg14328.description:
Boethius composed De Consolation Philosophiaein the sixth century A.D. while awaiting death by torture, condemned on a charge of plotting against Gothic rule, which he protested as manifestly unjust. Though a Christian, Boethius details the true end of life as the soul's knowledge of God, and consoles himself with the tenets of Greek philosophy, not with Christian precepts.

book:11810044.description: Horace's Satires not only handles moral topics with a persuasive air of sweet reason but also reveals much of the poet's own engaging personality and way of life. book:132876.description: Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus, 65-8 BCE) was born at Venusia, son of a freedman clerk who had him well educated at Rome and Athens. After 30 Horace knew and aided with his pen the emperor Augustus, who after Virgil's death...

book:web_a15799fb.description: A collection of satirical poems by the Roman poet Horace, also known as the Satires, first published around 35 BCE.
commentaries: Suetonius recounts that Augustus complained to Horace after reading his Sermones and finding no mention of himself.

book:8037448.description: Timeless meditations on the subjects of wine, parties, birthdays, love, and friendship, Horace's Odes, in the words of classicist Donald Carne-Ross, make the "commonplace notable, even luminous." commentaries: Augustine of Hippo references Zeller's book on the Stoics for further information.

book:1268768.description: Lucan's great poem, Pharsalia, recounts events surrounding the decisive battle fought near Pharsalus in 48 B.C. during the civil war between the forces of Pompey and Julius Caesar. Though the subject of this unfinished masterpiece is historical, many of its features are characteristic of epic poetry: Rousing battle scenes; tales of witches, monsters, and miracle; detailed catalogues; intricate similes; and speeches with a high degree of rhetorical elegance. However, Lucan's deft mix of humor and horror, of....

book:web_0e91675e.description: Epic poem by Lucan, also known as De Bello Civili, covering the civil war between Julius Caesar and Pompey the Great.

book:web_d40ebcbb.description: A historical monograph by the Roman historian Sallust, detailing the conspiracy of Catiline in 63 BC.
commentaries: Augustine of Hippo cites Sallust's work on the Catiline conspiracy as a source.

book:323202.description:
Alternate cover edition of ISBN 0140441328.
Sallust (86-c. 35 BC), who had various public offices in Rome & later a governorship in Africa, supported the political group known as the populares. He was a friend of Caesar & an opponent of Cicero. His history of the war against Jugurtha, King of Numidia, & his account of Catiline's conspiracy in 63 BC are his only complete works to survive; they were written in the years after Caesar's assassination.
commentaries: Niccolò Machiavelli references Sallust's account of the Catiline conspiracy as an example of how a republic can be slow to act against conspirators.

book:755218.description: Sallust (86-c. 35 bc) is the earliest Roman historian of whom complete works survive, a senator of the Roman Republic and younger contemporary of Cicero, Pompey and Julius Caesar. His Catiline's Wartells of the conspiracy in 63 bc led by L. Sergius Catilina, who plotted to assassinate numerous senators and take control of the government, but was thwarted by Cicero. book:817956.description: The African Q. Septimus Florens Tertullianus (ca. 150-222 CE), the great Christian writer, was born a soldier's son at Carthage, educated in Greek and Roman literature, philosophy, and medicine, studied law and became a pleader, remaining a clever and often tortuous arguer.
